title: Printing Spreads Like Wildfire
summary: After a war in Mainz in 1462, printers packed up their skills and moved to new cities all over Europe. Soon there were print shops in Rome, Venice, Paris and London, making beautiful new letters, small pocket books and the very first book in English. By the year 1500, millions of printed books existed, and they were getting cheaper every year.

sections.heading: A Night of Fire in Mainz
paragraphs: In the autumn of 1462, the city of Mainz was caught in the middle of a power struggle. Two rival churchmen both claimed to be Archbishop of Mainz, which in those days meant ruling a large territory, not just leading a church. One was Diether von Isenburg. The other was Adolph of Nassau, who had the support of the pope. Mainz had sided with Diether. On the night of 28 October 1462, Adolph's soldiers broke into the city. There was fighting in the streets, and houses were plundered and burned. Hundreds of people are thought to have died.

Afterwards, Adolph punished the townspeople who had opposed him. Many lost their property, and a large number of citizens were forced to leave the city. Among them, according to the Gutenberg Museum's history of the city, were workers from the print shops of Gutenberg and of Johann Fust and Peter Schoeffer. Printing in Mainz stopped for a while. Fust and Schoeffer, who had been busy printing beautiful books, seem to have printed almost nothing for around two or three years.

Imagine being one of those workers: a young compositor or pressman who had spent years learning the secret new craft, now suddenly without a job or a home. What did you have? Your skill. You knew how to cut punches, cast type, mix oily ink, set lines in a composing stick and work a press. In a world where hardly anyone else knew these things, that knowledge was worth a fortune. So printers did what skilled workers have always done. They went looking for cities that wanted what they could offer: rich trading towns full of merchants, university towns full of students and teachers, and cities with powerful churchmen who needed books.

Historians often tell the story of 1462 as the moment printing exploded out of Mainz, and it certainly helped. But it was not the only cause. Printing had already started to leave Mainz before the attack. In Strasbourg, Johannes Mentelin was printing a large Latin Bible by about 1460. In Bamberg, Albrecht Pfister printed books with woodcut pictures around 1460 to 1461, among the first printed books in German illustrated in this way. Some scholars think the effect of the sack has been exaggerated, since printing would probably have spread anyway once people saw how well it worked. The fairest way to put it is this: the sack of Mainz gave an extra push to a movement that was already beginning.

Whatever the exact cause, the results were astonishing. In 1460 printing was a rare skill found in only a handful of German towns. By 1500, only forty years later, printing presses had worked in more than 250 European towns and cities. Hundreds of print shops had opened and closed, and millions of printed books were in circulation. Let us follow some of those wandering printers on their journeys.

sections.heading: Over the Alps: Subiaco and Rome
paragraphs: The first printers to cross the Alps into Italy were two Germans, Konrad Sweynheym and Arnold Pannartz. Sweynheym had probably learned printing in Mainz, possibly in the Fust and Schoeffer workshop. Around 1464 or 1465 the pair settled not in a big city but in a quiet, beautiful spot in the hills east of Rome: the Benedictine monastery of Santa Scolastica at Subiaco. The monastery had many German monks, which may be why the two printers were welcomed there.

At Subiaco, in 1465, Sweynheym and Pannartz printed some of the first books ever made in Italy, including works by the ancient Roman writer Cicero and the early Christian author Lactantius. Their Lactantius, finished in October 1465, is the earliest printed book in Italy with an exact date. Their typeface was also interesting. Instead of the dark, pointed blackletter style of Gutenberg's Bible, they used a lighter, rounder letter inspired by the handwriting of Italian scholars. It was not yet a fully developed roman type like the letters you are reading now, but it was a step in that direction.

In 1467 the two printers moved to Rome itself, setting up in a house provided by a noble family, the Massimi. Rome was full of churchmen, scholars and visitors, and the printers turned out edition after edition of classical Latin authors and church writings. Another German, Ulrich Han from Ingolstadt, also started printing in Rome around the same time. According to the Gutenberg Museum, more than 40 print shops were set up in Rome before 1500, and about 25 of them were run by Germans.

Business was not easy, though. In 1472 Sweynheym and Pannartz sent a petition to Pope Sixtus IV asking for help. They explained that they had printed many books, but that thousands of copies were sitting unsold in their house and they were running out of money. This shows something important. Printing made books faster and cheaper to produce, but printers still had to find buyers. Printing too many copies of the same scholarly book for a small market could ruin you. Over the next decades, successful printers learned to choose titles more carefully, to work with booksellers who could ship books to faraway fairs and cities, and to print cheaper books that many more people would want.

sections.heading: Venice: Europe's Printing Capital
paragraphs: If you had wanted to see the busiest printing city in the world around 1490, you would have headed for Venice. This city of canals in northern Italy was one of the richest trading powers in Europe. Its merchant ships sailed all over the Mediterranean, its bankers had money to invest, paper mills operated in the region around it, and its famous university town, Padua, was close by. Venice was perfect for printing.

The first printer in Venice was another German, Johann of Speyer, sometimes called Johannes de Spira. He had been in Mainz around 1460 to 1461. In 1469 he printed an edition of Cicero's letters to his friends, the first printed book in Venice. That same year the Venetian government gave him a special privilege: for five years, nobody else was allowed to print books in Venice. This was one of the earliest printing privileges in Europe, a kind of early ancestor of patents and copyright. But Johann died in 1470, the privilege ended with him, and the city was suddenly open to anyone who wanted to try. Printers poured in.

One of the most famous was Nicolas Jenson, a Frenchman who had been master of the royal mint at Tours, where coins were made. According to a well-known account, King Charles VII of France sent him to Mainz in 1458 to learn the secrets of the new art. Jenson later settled in Venice and opened his shop in 1470. That year he printed a book by the early church historian Eusebius using a new roman typeface that printers and designers still admire today. Jenson's letters were clear, evenly spaced and beautifully balanced, with round shapes based on the handwriting of Italian humanist scholars. They made a clean break from the heavy blackletter style. More than 400 years later, the English designer William Morris praised Jenson's type and based his own Golden Type on it, and many modern typefaces have followed its example. By the late 1470s Jenson could run as many as twelve presses at once and had produced around 150 books.

Venice's printing industry grew enormous. Between 1469 and 1500, roughly 150 to 200 named printers worked in the city, and they produced around 3,500 to 3,800 known editions, more than 10 percent of all books printed in Europe in the 1400s and more than any other city. Venetian printers were especially famous for books in Greek and Hebrew, beautiful illustrated books, music printing and maps. In 1501 Ottaviano Petrucci printed there the first book of part music for several voices made with movable type. Erhard Ratdolt, a printer from Augsburg who worked in Venice, published a famous edition of the ancient Greek mathematician Euclid in 1482, one of the first printed books to include many geometry diagrams in its margins.

sections.heading: Aldus, Griffo and the Pocket Book
paragraphs: Aldus Manutius was born around 1450 in Bassiano, a small town south of Rome. He was not trained as a printer. He was a teacher and a scholar who loved ancient Greek, and he was worried that the great works of Greek literature, science and philosophy were scattered across rare handwritten copies that few people could ever see. His solution was to become a publisher. Around 1494, working with a businessman named Andrea Torresano, who had earlier bought Jenson's printing business, he set up a print shop in Venice. It became known as the Aldine Press.

The Aldine Press's first book appeared in 1495: a Greek grammar by Constantine Lascaris. Over the next years Aldus published a huge five-volume edition of Aristotle in Greek (1495 to 1498) and dozens of other ancient Greek texts, many printed for the very first time. Greek was very hard to print. It has its own alphabet, and its handwriting used many accents, breathing marks and joined letters, so a Greek font needed hundreds of different sorts. Aldus's Greek books helped scholars all over Europe study texts that had been almost unavailable in the West.

In 1499 the Aldine Press printed one of the most beautiful books of the whole century, a strange, dreamlike love story called the Hypnerotomachia Poliphili, with elegant woodcut pictures arranged carefully alongside the text. Book designers still study it today. But Aldus's most famous idea came two years later.

In 1501 he published the poems of the Roman poet Virgil in a new size: octavo. As you saw in the last part, an octavo is made by folding each big sheet three times, giving 8 leaves and 16 pages, so the book comes out small, roughly the size of a modern paperback. Before this, serious books of classical literature were usually large folios or quartos, often printed with long commentaries crowding around the text, and meant to sit on a desk or a lectern. Aldus's little octavos had plain text, no heavy commentary, and could be carried in a coat pocket or a saddlebag. A reader could take Virgil on a journey, read him in a garden, or study him by candlelight in a small room. Many historians see these books as distant ancestors of the modern paperback.

Aldus also printed these books in big runs. His 1501 Virgil was printed in about 1,000 copies, when 200 to 500 was more usual. Latin octavos from the Aldine Press cost about 30 soldi, a Venetian coin, which was much less than a big folio. Within a few years, the Aldine Press had published more than 100 editions. From 1502 its books carried a printer's mark showing a dolphin wrapped around an anchor, with the Latin motto festina lente, meaning 'make haste slowly'. The design became so famous that other printers copied it, and pirate editions of Aldine books, printed in Lyon in France and elsewhere, appeared within months.
Aldus's octavos needed one more ingredient: a new, space-saving kind of letter.

To fit lots of text onto a small page, Aldus needed a letter that was narrow and elegant. He turned to a brilliant punchcutter named Francesco Griffo, from Bologna. A punchcutter, as you saw in earlier parts, was the craftsman who carved each letter in reverse on the tip of a steel punch, the very first step in making type. Griffo had already cut Aldus's Greek and roman typefaces, including the roman letters used in a 1496 book by the scholar Pietro Bembo, which inspired a modern typeface still called Bembo.

For the new pocket books, Griffo cut a slanted, flowing typeface that copied the quick, joined-up handwriting used by Italian scholars of the time. It first appeared in a few words in a book of letters by Saint Catherine of Siena in 1500, and then for a whole book in the octavo Virgil of 1501. This was italic type, named after Italy. Each letter was narrow, and the font included many joined letter pairs, so more words fitted on each line, and the page looked like fine handwriting.

There are two surprises about the first italic. First, it was not used the way we use italics today, to stress a word or mark a book title. Aldus printed entire books in it. Only later did printers begin mixing italic and roman type on the same page, using italic for emphasis. Second, the first italic had no slanted capital letters. Its capitals were small upright roman capitals, and slanted italic capitals came only later.

Aldus was so proud of the new type that he asked the government of Venice for protection. The Venetian Senate gave him an exclusive privilege to use it, and popes confirmed his rights too. But type could be copied, and imitations appeared within a year or two. Aldus and Griffo also quarreled, apparently over credit and money, and Griffo left Venice. He worked for other printers and later printed small books of his own in Bologna, but much of his later life is unclear, and the last records of him date from around 1518.

sections.heading: Paris, Lyon and Beyond
paragraphs: While Italy raced ahead, printing was spreading in every direction. In Paris, two scholars at the Sorbonne, the city's famous college of theology, wanted good printed books for students and teachers. In 1470 they invited three German printers, Ulrich Gering, Martin Crantz and Michael Friburger, to set up a press inside the college buildings. Their first book was a collection of model letters to teach students how to write elegant Latin. Paris soon became one of Europe's great printing centers, along with Lyon, an important trading city on the Rhône River where printing began in 1473. Lyon, with its big trade fairs, became famous for books sold to merchants and ordinary readers, often in French.

Printers also reached the Low Countries and the Iberian Peninsula. Utrecht and other Dutch towns had presses by 1473. In Spain, the German printer Lambert Palmart was working in Valencia by about 1473, and in 1490 Nicolaus Spindeler printed the famous Valencian adventure story Tirant lo Blanch there. Further east, Andreas Hess printed in Buda, in Hungary, in the early 1470s, and Kasper Straube printed in Kraków, in Poland, around 1473 to 1477.

Jewish printers made important contributions too, printing Hebrew Bibles, prayer books and works of law and philosophy. Hebrew printing flourished in Italy and on the Iberian Peninsula in the 1470s and 1480s. When Jews were forced to leave Spain in 1492 and Portugal in 1497, some printers carried their skills to new homes. In Istanbul, capital of the Ottoman Empire, the brothers David and Samuel ibn Nahmias printed a Hebrew book of Jewish law, and many historians date it to 1493, though some argue for a few years later. It was the first book printed in the Ottoman Empire.

Most of these first printers were Germans. All over Europe, early print shops were run by men with names like Ulrich, Konrad, Johann and Michael, often working far from home. Because type was heavy but a press could be built by any good carpenter, a printer could set up almost anywhere he found customers and paper. If the business failed, or the local ruler became unfriendly, he could pack up his punches, matrices and some type and move on to the next town.

sections.heading: William Caxton Brings Printing to England
paragraphs: The man who brought printing to England did not start out as a printer at all. William Caxton was born in Kent, in south-east England, around 1422. As a young man, in 1438, he was apprenticed to a rich London mercer, a merchant who traded in fine cloth. By around 1453 he was living in Bruges, in today's Belgium, one of the busiest trading cities in northern Europe. He did well there and became governor of the community of English merchants in the Low Countries, an important and respected position. He also came to know Margaret of York, sister of the English King Edward IV, who married the powerful Duke of Burgundy in 1468.

Caxton loved books and liked translating French romances into English. He found that people kept asking for copies of his translation of a long French story about the Trojan War. Copying it by hand was exhausting; he wrote that his pen was worn, his hand weary and his eyes dimmed from so much writing. During a stay in Cologne in Germany in 1471 and 1472, where printing was already well established, he learned how the new art worked. Back in Bruges, with the help of a scribe and printer named Colard Mansion, he set up a press.

Around 1473 or 1474, Caxton printed his own translation, The Recuyell of the Historyes of Troye, meaning 'collection of the stories of Troy'. It is the first book ever printed in the English language, and it was printed not in England but in Bruges. A copy sold at auction in London in 2014 for over one million pounds.

In 1476 Caxton moved back to England and set up a press in Westminster, near Westminster Abbey and the royal palace, close to the people who could afford books: courtiers, lawyers, nobles and churchmen. It was England's first printing press. One of his first big books there was Geoffrey Chaucer's Canterbury Tales, the great collection of stories told by pilgrims on their way to Canterbury, written about 80 years earlier. In 1477 he printed The Dictes or Sayengis of the Philosophres, the earliest book printed in England with an exact printed date. Later came an English Aesop's Fables (1484) and Thomas Malory's Le Morte d'Arthur (1485), the tales of King Arthur and his knights. Altogether Caxton printed more than 100 different works, most of them in English.

Caxton also had a problem: English was not yet one language with fixed spellings. People in different parts of England spoke and wrote very differently. In the introduction to one of his later books, Caxton told a story about some merchants travelling down the River Thames who stopped at a farmhouse and asked for 'egges'. The woman of the house said she did not understand French. Another traveler asked for 'eyren', and she understood at once, because both words meant eggs in different English dialects. Caxton asked his readers which word a printer should use. By printing mostly in the English of London and the court, Caxton and the printers after him helped slowly push English toward a more standard form. When Caxton died, around 1491 or 1492, his assistant Wynkyn de Worde took over the business and later moved it to Fleet Street in London, which became famous for printing and newspapers for centuries.

sections.heading: Cradle Books: The Incunabula
paragraphs: Book experts have a special name for the very first printed books in Europe. Books printed before the year 1501 are called incunabula, or incunables. The word comes from Latin and originally meant swaddling clothes, the cloth wrapped around a newborn baby, or a cradle. A Dutch scholar named Hadrianus Junius used it in a book written in 1569 to describe printing's earliest days. So incunabula are 'cradle books', from the time when printing was still a baby.

The cut-off of 1501 is just a convenient round number. Libraries around the world have worked together to list every known incunabulum. The Incunabula Short Title Catalogue, kept by the British Library and its partners, records around 30,000 different editions from this period, and new discoveries still turn up. Historians estimate that all these editions together produced somewhere between about 8 and 20 million copies, depending on how many copies they think were printed of each. Typical print runs were often a few hundred copies, though some popular books were printed in a thousand or more.

Around 550,000 individual copies of incunabula are thought to survive in libraries and private collections today, a remarkable number for objects more than 500 years old. Some editions survive in hundreds of copies, but others are known only from a single battered copy or a few loose pages found inside the binding of a later book. Probably many editions have disappeared entirely, especially cheap and popular things like schoolbooks, calendars and pamphlets that were read until they fell apart.

Incunabula are full of clues to the people who made and used them. Many look a lot like manuscripts, because early printers copied the look of handwritten books their customers were used to. Big capital letters at the start of chapters were often left blank for an artist to paint in by hand, and red headings were added later with a pen. There was usually no title page at first. Instead, details about the printer, the place and the date were printed at the end, in a short note called a colophon. Title pages, page numbers and printers' marks slowly became normal by around 1500. Readers' notes in the margins, owners' names and old prices written inside the covers help historians learn who bought these books and how they read them.

sections.heading: Cheaper Books for More Readers
paragraphs: Did printing really make books cheaper? Yes, though not all at once. The first printed books of the 1460s often cost as much as fine manuscripts. In Venice, a study of book prices found that they began falling in the 1470s and then dropped sharply in the 1480s, a fall that continued into the 1490s. As more printers competed and print runs grew, prices came down.

We have an amazing window into this world thanks to an account book kept by a Venetian bookseller named Francesco de Madiis between 1484 and 1488. It is known as the Zornale, Venetian for 'daybook', and it records about 7,000 sales covering around 25,000 books. It shows that well over a thousand sales were for less than the daily wage of an ordinary builder, about 15 soldi. The cheapest best-seller was a 16-page reading book for children, a little psalter used to learn to read, which sold 659 copies at just 4 soldi each. A typical copy of a classical author might cost 20 to 40 soldi, roughly a master builder's pay for a day or two. At the top end, a giant 1,628-page Bible with commentary cost 1,240 soldi, the same as a handwritten prayer book. So big, fancy books were still expensive, but small books were now within reach of many working people.

Printers also discovered that they could sell many new kinds of books. Early presses produced Latin grammars for schoolchildren, especially the short grammar by Donatus, which was printed again and again. They printed calendars and almanacs telling people about holy days and the phases of the Moon. They printed law books for lawyers, medical books for doctors, prayer books for families, and dictionaries for students. They printed travel books, like Bernhard von Breydenbach's illustrated account of a pilgrimage to Jerusalem (1486), and grand illustrated histories, like the Nuremberg Chronicle of 1493, with more than 1,800 woodcut pictures printed from about 650 woodblocks. They printed stories, poems and romances in everyday languages, from Italian and French to German, Spanish, Dutch and English, not just in Latin.

Governments and churches used printing too. They printed laws, announcements, forms and the indulgence certificates you met in earlier parts. Printing could spread news of a battle, a new decree or a discovery across hundreds of miles in a few weeks. In 1493, for example, a letter by Christopher Columbus describing his first voyage was printed in Spain and then quickly reprinted in Latin and other languages in cities such as Rome, Basel, Paris and Antwerp.

By 1500, then, Europe had changed in a quiet but enormous way. Instead of a few hundred books in a great library, a single city could have thousands of copies of hundreds of titles for sale. Scholars far apart could read the same edition, with the same words on the same page. More people could own a book, and more people had a reason to learn to read. Cheap, fast printing meant new ideas could now spread faster than anyone could stop them, and an angry monk was about to prove it.

deepDive:
How do historians know how many books were printed before 1501? Nobody kept a master list at the time, so the numbers are built up from the books that survive. Two great catalogues do most of the work: the Incunabula Short Title Catalogue (ISTC), now hosted by the Consortium of European Research Libraries, and the German Gesamtkatalog der Wiegendrucke ('complete catalogue of cradle prints'). Together they list around 28,000 to 30,000 editions, depending on how items are counted and on whether a few undated books really belong before 1501. Venice alone accounts for well over 3,500 of them, more than any other city.

Turning editions into copies is harder. If an average print run was about 300 copies, 30,000 editions would mean roughly 9 million books; if it was closer to 500, the total rises to about 15 million. Hence the wide range, often quoted as about 8 to 20 million copies. Around 550,000 copies survive, but survival is very uneven. Big, expensive Latin folios were treasured by libraries, while cheap grammars, almanacs, broadsides and pamphlets were read to pieces. Some editions are known only from scraps recycled inside later bindings, and many have surely vanished without trace, so the real number of editions was certainly higher than the catalogues show.

The count of printing towns varies too. Different studies give figures from about 236 to 282 places by 1500, depending on whether they count a town where one wandering printer made one book, or only towns with a lasting press. What everyone agrees on is the shape of the story: a handful of German towns around 1460, more than a hundred places by the early 1480s, and well over 250 by 1500, with Italy and Germany far ahead of the rest.

Economic historians are also interested in prices and law. The Zornale of Francesco de Madiis shows books ranging from a few soldi to over a thousand, letting researchers compare book prices with wages for the first time. The Venetian privileges, such as Johann of Speyer's five-year monopoly in 1469 and Aldus's protection for his italic type, are studied as early experiments in what we now call intellectual property. They show governments trying, not always successfully, to reward inventors while still letting a new industry grow.
funFact: The first book ever printed in English, Caxton's Recuyell of the Historyes of Troye, was printed in Bruges in today's Belgium, not in England.
